articles.title: From 5L to 5000L: the engineering behind seamless bioreactor scale-up
articles.text:
Articles From 5L to 5000L: the engineering behind seamless bioreactor scale-up Scaling up used to mean starting over. With consistent geometry and mixing design, bench-to-commercial bioreactor translation is becoming predictable. Written by Trevor J Henderson Trevor J Henderson Trevor Henderson is the Creative Services Director for the Laboratory Products Group at LabX Media Group. With over two decades of experience, he specializes in scientific and technical writing, editing, View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 4, 2026 | 7 min read The challenge of bioreactor scale-up is not biological: cells do not know how large the vessel around them is. The challenge is hydrodynamic. Maintaining consistent oxygen transfer, mixing uniformity, and shear stress profiles as vessel volume increases by three orders of magnitude is the engineering problem that scale-up criteria, geometric design, and scale-down modeling are all built to solve. Flow (2026) Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Highlights in this article Why scale-up fails: the physics of increasing volume The engineering criteria of bioreactor scale-up Geometric similarity: engineering predictability into the vessel design Scale-down models: predicting commercial behavior at bench scale N-1 perfusion: redefining the inoculation density Process analytical technology in scale-up verification Most bioreactor scale-up failures are not scientific failures. They are engineering failures. The biology that worked at 5 liters, including the cell line, the media, the feeding strategy, and the dissolved oxygen setpoint, is sound. What changes between the bench bioreactor and the 2,000-liter production vessel is the physics of the environment surrounding those cells, and if those changes are not anticipated and engineered for, the process that looked excellent at small scale will behave unexpectedly at large scale. The parameters that govern cell culture productivity do not scale linearly with volume. Mixing time, oxygen transfer rate, CO2 accumulation, and shear stress distribution all change in ways that can stress cells, alter product quality attributes, and create batch-to-batch variability that raises regulatory questions. Understanding how and why these parameters change and designing scale-up strategies to control them is the technical foundation of predictable scale-up. This article covers the engineering principles of bioreactor scale-up, from the dimensionless criteria used to design consistent hydrodynamic environments to the role of N-1 perfusion in redefining inoculation density. For the facility design context in which this scale-up engineering operates, see the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities , and for the broader bioprocessing lifecycle from development through commercial manufacturing, see the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . Continue reading below... Articles Improving HLA-informed cell therapy development Explore engineered cellular models and screening approaches designed to support more targeted evaluation of adoptive cell therapies. Read More Why scale-up fails: the physics of increasing volume When a bioreactor volume increases by a factor of 1,000, from 5 liters to 5,000 liters, the linear dimensions of the vessel increase by only the cube root of 1,000, approximately 10-fold. That geometric relationship governs everything about how the hydrodynamics of the culture change, and most of those changes make the engineering problem harder. Mixing time, the time required for a pulse addition to be uniformly distributed throughout the vessel, increases with scale under constant volumetric power input. In a 5-liter bioreactor, a base pulse from the pH control loop may homogenize in seconds. In a 2,000-liter vessel, the same pulse may create a transient pH gradient that exposes cells in the vicinity of the addition point to conditions outside the setpoint range for tens of seconds before bulk mixing restores uniformity. Cells exposed to repeated pH excursions can shift glycosylation patterns and charge variant profiles, potentially affecting critical quality attributes of the drug substance. Dissolved CO2 accumulation is another scale-dependent challenge. In large-scale bioreactors, the hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of a tall vessel increases the partial pressure of dissolved CO2 beyond levels typically encountered at bench scale, and bubbles have a longer residence time in the culture as they rise through a deeper liquid column. Elevated pCO2 can inhibit cell growth and alter glycosylation, and the CO2 stripping strategy that works at 5 liters may be insufficient at 2,000 liters. Shear stress distribution also changes. Impeller tip speed, which correlates with the shear forces cells experience near the agitator, scales with impeller diameter and rotation speed. Maintaining a constant tip speed at large scale while also maintaining adequate mixing requires impeller design choices that become increasingly complex as vessel volume increases. Research published in Biotechnology Progress in 2025 confirmed that hydrodynamic conditions, including volumetric power input, impeller configuration, and aeration strategy, are among the most significant determinants of production yield during CHO fed-batch scale-up, and that no single criterion adequately captures the full complexity of the scale-up problem. The engineering criteria of bioreactor scale-up Scale-up engineering uses dimensionless or volume-normalized criteria to design bioreactor operating conditions that maintain consistent hydrodynamic environments as vessel scale increases. No single criterion perfectly captures the full complexity of scale-up, and in practice, scale-up engineers must choose which criterion to prioritize based on the process requirements and the cell line's specific sensitivities. Criterion What it controls How it is maintained Key trade-off at large scale P/V (volumetric power input) Mixing energy per unit volume; shear stress distribution Constant agitation power per unit volume as vessel scale increases Maintaining P/V at large scale requires higher tip speeds, increasing shear stress risk for sensitive cell lines kLa (oxygen transfer coefficient) Rate of oxygen delivery from gas to culture; critical at high viable cell density Combined adjustment of agitation rate, sparge gas flow, and sparger design to maintain target kLa Higher gas flows increase foaming and CO2 stripping; bubble coalescence behavior changes with vessel geometry Tip speed Local shear near impeller blade; primary shear stress experienced by cells Constant impeller peripheral velocity across scales Conflicts with P/V criterion at large scale; requires impeller diameter and geometry optimization Mixing time (tm) Time for complete homogenization; determines pH and DO gradient severity Geometric similarity and optimized impeller configuration Inherently increases with volume; spatial heterogeneity in large bioreactors can affect critical quality attributes vvm (volumetric gas flow rate) Total gas delivery per unit culture volume; CO2 stripping capacity Constant gas volume per culture volume per minute CO2 accumulates with increasing vessel height; bubble behavior changes with hydrostatic pressure at depth In practice, maintaining constant P/V is the most widely used primary scale-up criterion for mammalian cell culture because it most directly controls the mixing environment and is most predictive of cell culture performance. kLa is typically verified as a secondary criterion to confirm adequate oxygen delivery at the target agitation and gassing conditions. Tip speed is monitored as a constraint: if the tip speed required to maintain P/V at large scale exceeds the shear sensitivity threshold of the cell line, the impeller design must be revised. Continue reading below... Articles DNA synthesis 101: steps, enzymes, and importance Explore the principles, technologies, and applications that enable scientists to design and build DNA for research, biotechnology, and therapeutic development. Read More Geometric similarity: engineering predictability into the vessel design The most reliable foundation for predictable scale-up is geometric similarity across the full volume range of a bioreactor platform. When key geometric ratios, including the height-to-diameter ratio of the vessel (H/D), the ratio of impeller diameter to tank diameter (d/D), and the impeller off-bottom clearance, are held constant from 5 liters to 5,000 liters, the dimensionless hydrodynamic behavior of the culture scales predictably. The kLa, mixing time, and shear profiles calculated or measured at bench scale will translate to large scale without requiring empirical re-optimization of every operating parameter. This principle is why modern single-use bioreactor platforms designed for process development through commercial manufacturing maintain consistent geometric ratios across their volume range. A development bioreactor and a production bioreactor from the same platform family, operating at the same impeller rotation speed in revolutions per minute per liter of culture, will produce similar hydrodynamic environments because the geometry that generates those environments is consistent. Scale-up becomes a matter of calculating the correct operating parameters for the new volume, rather than re-characterizing the process from scratch. For single-use bioreactors, bag geometry is as important as vessel geometry. The working volume fraction of the bag, the aspect ratio of the inflated bag at maximum fill, and the film architecture, meaning the layered polymer construction of the bag itself, affect both the hydrodynamic environment inside the vessel and the extractables profile of the bag material in contact with the drug substance. Consistent film specifications across a platform's volume range are a prerequisite for assuming that extractables data generated at small scale will be representative of large-scale production conditions. Scale-down models: predicting commercial behavior at bench scale Designing a scale-down model that accurately predicts the behavior of a large-scale production bioreactor is one of the most valuable investments a process development team can make. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Biological Engineering documented successful scale-up of CHO cell cultures across three orders of magnitude, from 96-well microtiter plates through stirred-tank bioreactors, by carefully matching oxygen transfer rates and mixing conditions at each scale. The study confirmed that oxygen transfer rate, not simply agitation speed, is the critical parameter for maintaining cell culture performance across scale transitions. A scale-down model for a 2,000-liter production bioreactor is typically a 10- to 15-liter bioreactor operated to mimic the kLa, mixing time, and pH and DO control dynamics of the large-scale vessel. For processes sensitive to pH heterogeneity, scale-down heterogeneity models deliberately introduce controlled pH or dissolved oxygen gradients that simulate the transient excursions cells experience in a large vessel where base pulses do not distribute instantaneously. These models allow process development scientists to evaluate the impact of large-scale heterogeneity on cell performance and product quality without consuming the time and resources of a full-scale run. Continue reading below... Infographics How to run a successful high-throughput screening campaign Learn the key assay design principles and workflow considerations that help support robust, scalable, and reliable high-throughput screening campaigns. Read More Miniaturized bioreactor systems operating at 15 to 250 milliliters enable high-throughput screening of operating conditions, cell lines, and media formulations with consistent hydrodynamic control in a parallel format. These systems are most valuable in early process development, where large numbers of conditions must be evaluated quickly. Their role in scale-up validation is more limited: they can confirm parameter sensitivity and establish media and feeding optima, but a 15-milliliter vessel cannot faithfully reproduce the CO2 accumulation and mixing time dynamics of a 2,000-liter production bioreactor. N-1 perfusion: redefining the inoculation density Conventional fed-batch bioreactor scale-up begins with inoculation at a viable cell density of approximately 0.5 million cells per milliliter. The culture then spends the first three to five days of the production run in a growth phase, building cell density before peak productivity is reached. That growth phase consumes bioreactor time, media, and production capacity without generating product, and any variability in the health or density of the seed material propagates directly into production bioreactor performance. N-1 perfusion changes this starting point. By running the final seed train stage in perfusion mode, continuously exchanging spent media with fresh media while retaining cells in the vessel, the N-1 bioreactor can accumulate viable cell density far beyond what is achievable in a standard batch seed. Research from Bristol Myers Squibb published in Bioengineering in 2022 demonstrated that N-1 perfusion with in-line capacitance probe control achieved 4.5-fold higher inoculation VCD than conventional batch N-1 seeding, delivering 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter to the production bioreactor versus the standard 0.5 million cells per milliliter. The production consequences are significant. A production bioreactor inoculated at 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter bypasses the slow growth phase, reaching peak viable cell density faster, maintaining higher peak VCD for longer, and generating proportionally more product in the same calendar time. A 2024 study published in Biotechnology Progress demonstrated that N-1 perfusion-enabled high inoculation density processes achieved an average 85% titer increase and 132% space-time yield increase compared to conventional low-inoculation-density fed-batch processes across six CHO cell lines expressing three different monoclonal antibodies. Integrating N-1 perfusion into scale-up design also improves the uniformity of seed material delivered to the production bioreactor, reducing run-to-run variability that can otherwise be attributed to variation in the physiological state of the inoculum rather than to true process variability at production scale. Process analytical technology in scale-up verification Process analytical technology (PAT) bridges the bench and commercial scale by providing real-time, in-process measurements of the critical parameters that scale-up engineering is designed to control. The FDA's PAT framework guidance , first published in 2004, explicitly supports the use of real-time quality monitoring rather than end-product testing and encouraged manufacturers to build process understanding through in-line and on-line measurement systems. That regulatory support has enabled the adoption of a generation of PAT tools that are now routinely deployed in both scale-down models and production bioreactors. Continue reading below... Application Note Scaling neuronal activity profiling with semi-automated electrophysiology Advanced microelectrode array and liquid handling technologies make neuronal culture screening more consistent and easier to scale. Read More In scale-up verification, PAT serves two complementary functions. At small scale, it establishes multivariate models that correlate measured process signals with cell culture performance and product quality outcomes. At large scale, it confirms that the critical process parameters defined during small-scale development are being maintained within their designed ranges, and that the performance the models predict at small scale is actually being achieved at production scale. Key PAT tools in bioreactor scale-up verification include in-line Raman spectroscopy for real-time glucose, lactate, and product concentration measurement; near-infrared spectroscopy for cell density and metabolite monitoring; and capacitance probes for viable cell density estimation without sampling. The integration of multiple PAT data streams into a unified process monitoring platform enables real-time decisions about feeding, pH adjustment, and harvest timing that would otherwise depend on discrete offline measurements taken hours apart. For context on how PAT and digital manufacturing tools integrate into the broader Pharma 4.0 framework, see the related coverage in the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . For the role of purification and downstream scale-up as the continuation of the upstream scale-up engineering challenge, see the coverage of purification breakthroughs promising faster biologic development . This article was produced under Drug Discovery News' AI Editorial Guidelines Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is bioreactor scale-up? Bioreactor scale-up is the process of translating a cell culture manufacturing process from a small development-scale bioreactor to progressively larger vessels, ultimately reaching commercial production scale. The goal is to maintain the same hydrodynamic environment, including oxygen transfer rate, mixing uniformity, and shear stress distribution, at each larger scale so that cell culture performance and product quality attributes are preserved. Scale-up spans from bench-scale bioreactors of 5 to 15 liters in early development through clinical-scale vessels of 50 to 500 liters and production-scale vessels of 500 to 5,000 liters. What scale-up criteria are used to design consistent bioreactor environments? The most commonly used scale-up criteria in mammalian cell culture are volumetric power input (P/V), which maintains consistent mixing energy per unit volume; the oxygen transfer coefficient (kLa), which maintains consistent oxygen delivery; and tip speed, which maintains consistent shear stress near the impeller. Mixing time is monitored as a key outcome of the design, and volumetric gas flow rate (vvm) is maintained to ensure adequate CO2 stripping. No single criterion perfectly captures all aspects of scale-up, and process engineers must balance these criteria based on the specific sensitivities of their cell line and process. Why does pH become heterogeneous in large-scale bioreactors? In large-scale bioreactors, the base solution added by the pH control loop takes time to distribute throughout the vessel after each pulse addition. During that mixing time, the region near the addition point experiences a transient pH elevation before bulk mixing restores uniformity. In a 5-liter bioreactor, mixing may be complete in seconds. In a 2,000-liter vessel, mixing time under equivalent volumetric power input is longer, creating more significant and more prolonged pH gradients. Cells repeatedly exposed to these transient excursions can experience physiological stress that shifts glycosylation patterns and charge variant profiles, affecting critical quality attributes of the drug substance. What is N-1 perfusion and how does it improve bioreactor scale-up? N-1 perfusion runs the final stage of the seed train in perfusion mode, continuously exchanging spent media for fresh media while retaining cells in the vessel, allowing the seed culture to accumulate viable cell densities of 20 to 80 million cells per milliliter before inoculating the production bioreactor. Conventional batch N-1 seeding delivers inoculation densities of approximately 0.5 million cells per milliliter to the production bioreactor. N-1 perfusion has been shown to enable inoculation at 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter, a four- to 20-fold improvement that shortens the production bioreactor growth phase, increases peak viable cell density, and improves volumetric productivity. Published studies report titer increases of 85% or more from N-1 perfusion-enabled high inoculation density processes. What makes a good scale-down model for a production bioreactor? A good scale-down model matches the key hydrodynamic parameters of the large-scale production bioreactor, including kLa, mixing time, and the CO2 stripping characteristics of the gassing system, at a volume small enough to run in parallel with other development experiments. Beyond basic hydrodynamic matching, effective scale-down models for large-scale processes often incorporate deliberate pH or dissolved oxygen gradients that simulate the heterogeneity cells experience in large vessels, allowing development scientists to evaluate the impact of large-scale mixing limitations on cell performance and product quality without conducting a full-scale run. How does geometric similarity support bioreactor scale-up? Geometric similarity means maintaining consistent ratios of key vessel dimensions, including the vessel height-to-diameter ratio, the ratio of impeller diameter to vessel diameter, and impeller clearance from the vessel bottom, across all scales of a bioreactor platform. When these ratios are held constant, the dimensionless hydrodynamic behavior of the culture scales predictably with volume. The kLa, mixing time, and shear profiles at bench scale translate reliably to large scale, and operating conditions for new volumes can be calculated rather than empirically re-characterized from scratch. This is why bioreactor platforms designed with consistent geometry across their volume range provide more predictable scale-up than platforms where geometry varies by scale. Feb 10, 2026 | 8 min read Exploring how AI interprets cellular images to speed up drug discovery. credit: istock.com/Spectral-Design Download PDF Jonathan Sexton studies drug-induced liver injury and liver organoids, using high-content imaging, cell painting, and AI/ML to advance drug discovery. Credit: Jonathan Sexton Drug discovery is entering an era defined by unprecedented resolution in understanding cellular behavior. Traditional approaches often focus on one or a few biomarkers, giving a narrow view of how a compound affects cells. But recent advances in high-content imaging and computational biology are enabling a more holistic perspective — capturing the complexity of cellular responses in a single experiment. One technique at the forefront of this shift is Cell Painting, a morphological profiling assay that visualizes multiple cellular structures simultaneously using fluorescent dyes. By generating rich, high-dimensional data on organelle organization, shape, and texture, Cell Painting moves beyond hypothesis-driven screening, offering an unbiased window into cellular phenotypes. This allows researchers not only to identify potential drug effects and toxicity earlier but also to uncover unexpected mechanisms of action and opportunities for drug repurposing. To explore how Cell Painting is reshaping the landscape of drug discovery, DDN spoke with Jonathan Sexton , Associate Professor of Internal Medicine and Medicinal Chemistry at the University of Michigan, about the science behind the method, its practical applications in the lab, and the challenges and opportunities it presents for translating cellular insights into safer, more effective therapeutics. What is Cell Painting and why is it important for drug discovery? Cell Painting is a morphological profiling assay that uses a multiplexed set of fluorescent dyes to visualize specific cellular compartments — nucleus, nucleoli, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, cytoskeleton, and plasma membrane — simultaneously. What makes it fundamentally different from traditional high-content screening is its unbiased, hypothesis-free nature. Rather than designing an assay around a specific target or biomarker, we let the biology speak for itself. In drug discovery, this shift in philosophy is transformative. Instead of asking "does this drug inhibit kinase X?" we ask "what is the comprehensive cellular response to this compound?" This approach is particularly powerful for drug repurposing, one of my core research focuses, because compounds with unexpected activities in one disease context often reveal therapeutic potential in another. The morphological fingerprint can identify novel mechanisms of action, flag early toxicity signals, and cluster structurally dissimilar compounds that share biological effects, all from a single assay. How does Cell Painting differentiate from traditional phenotypic assays in terms of data richness and predictive power? Traditional phenotypic assays typically measure a handful of endpoints — viability, a reporter signal, perhaps a biomarker intensity or protein translocation event. They answer narrow questions but can miss the broader cellular context. Cell Painting extracts thousands of morphological features per cell: size, shape, texture, intensity distributions, spatial relationships between organelles, etc. A single well can yield millions of measurements. This dimensionality fundamentally changes what's predictable. In my work on drug-induced liver injury using patient-derived liver organoids, for example, we can detect organelle-level perturbations — mitochondrial fragmentation, ER stress patterns, phospholipidosis signatures — long before they manifest as overt toxicity. Compounds that look identical in a viability assay may have completely distinct Cell Painting profiles, revealing different mechanisms and different risk profiles. The technique effectively converts microscopy images into high-dimensional, computable biological data that machine learning (ML) models can leverage for predictions we could not make by visual inspection alone. How is Cell Painting used in your lab? In my lab, Cell Painting serves as a primary screening modality, but we've adapted it in ways that extend well beyond standard implementations. Mechanism of action discovery: We compare novel compound fingerprints against annotated reference libraries — including the JUMP-CP consortium data — to generate mechanistic hypotheses. This is particularly valuable for repurposing candidates where the original indication tells us little about potential new uses. Patient-derived organoid platforms: We've moved beyond immortalized cell lines to apply Cell Painting to intestinal and hepatic organoids derived from patient tissue. This is technically demanding — 3D structures require different staining penetration strategies and more sophisticated segmentation — but it bridges the gap between throughput and physiological relevance. AI/ML pipeline development: We use the rich Cell Painting datasets to train ML models that can detect subtle phenotypic changes invisible to the human eye. In our work on drug-induced liver injury (DILI), we are developing classifiers that predict clinical hepatotoxicity by analyzing morphological signatures in patient-derived liver cells. These models accurately identify drugs with known DILI risk. For example, using our approach, we were able to detect significant liver toxicity in several drugs that recently failed clinical trials, including inarigivir for chronic hepatitis B. The models revealed that its toxicity was driven by mitochondrial damage, highlighting how ML predictions can uncover specific mechanisms of harm. Barrier function prediction: One of our current projects uses machine vision to predict functional outcomes in intestinal organoids for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We have developed models that can accurately detect leaky gut, a condition where the intestinal barrier is compromised, allowing bacterial antigens to cross into the body and trigger inflammation — a key driver of IBD. By linking Cell Painting morphological features with measurements of barrier integrity (transepithelial electrical resistance), we created a predictive model that can guide drug discovery for IBD by identifying compounds that improve intestinal barrier function. What are some of the challenges or limitations of working with Cell Painting today? Several practical challenges persist despite the technique's maturation: Data infrastructure: A single large screen generates terabytes of images and hundreds of gigabytes of tabular data. We run our analysis using CellProfiler pipelines that output parquet files for downstream processing, but storage, versioning, and compute resources remain significant operational challenges. Batch effects: Cell Painting is very sensitive to experimental variation — staining duration, reagent lots, cell passage, even plate position effects. These batch effects can obscure true biological signals. We've invested heavily in normalization strategies and plate design to mitigate this, but it requires constant vigilance. Biological interpretation: We can extract a feature called "radial distribution of ER intensity at 50 percent radius" and detect how they change in response to a compound, but interpreting what these changes mean biologically remains challenging. The field is improving at linking specific feature patterns to known cellular processes, but much work remains. Combining Cell Painting with high-throughput transcriptomics can help reveal the underlying mechanisms, but it takes significant expertise to translate these data into a clear, interpretable molecular mechanism of action. Translating to complex models: Applying standardized Cell Painting protocols to organoids introduces new variables: penetration depth, optical sectioning requirements, segmentation of irregular 3D structures. The protocols that work beautifully in 2D monolayers require substantial optimization for our 3D patient-derived organoid systems. Cell Painting as a technique is around a decade old now. How has this tool improved over that time? The evolution has been remarkable, driven by improvements in high-content imaging hardware, biology and chemistry tools, and advancements in computational approaches for analysis. Imaging throughput: We use modern high-content imaging systems, specifically the Yokogawa Cell Voyager 8000 (CV8000), which allow rapid collection of high-quality images. The CV8000 uses water immersion objective lenses that greatly improve spatial resolution and signal-to-background ratios, and its four scientific CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) cameras capture four channels at the same time. Older Nipkow confocal spinning disc systems, by contrast, suffered from a drastic loss of signal that made them unusable for dyes/stains that weren’t very bright. The Yokogawa dual microlens spinning disc focuses light more efficiently through the pinholes, producing stronger signals even from weaker dyes. This lets us image faster, achieve higher resolution, and maintain robust signal intensity without compromise. 3D model compatibility: The adaptation to organoids and spheroids represents perhaps the most important biological advance. Early Cell Painting was validated exclusively in 2D immortalized lines. We're now successfully applying it to patient-derived 3D cultures, which introduces challenges in staining penetration and confocal imaging requirements but gains physiological relevance that dramatically improves translational value. Reagent improvements: Dye formulations are now more stable, and innovations like the Mitsui gas-permeable InnoCell plates — which we are testing for organoid experiments — help maintain high-quality 3D structures across large-scale screens. Analysis infrastructure: Nuclear and cellular segmentation has improved dramatically thanks to neural networks such as the CellPose 4 SAM model, which can achieve nearly perfect segmentation automatically, without any user input. Additionally, the JUMP-CP consortium has established reference datasets and standardized analysis workflows that didn’t exist five years ago, greatly improving our ability to compare data across instruments and batches. At the same time, CellProfiler has matured, and the field has developed widely accepted approaches for normalization and quality control. How do you see Cell Painting integrating with omics technologies such as transcriptomics, proteomics, or metabolomics to create a more holistic view of cellular states? Cell Painting provides something the omics technologies cannot: direct visualization of the phenotypic outcome of a perturbation, whether that be a small molecule drug or a genetic perturbation like CRISPR interference. Transcriptomics captures what the cell plans to do, proteomics informs what machinery the cell has available, and metabolomics indicates what reactions are occurring. Cell Painting shows the phenotypic result of a perturbation that anchors the analysis of other omics technologies with visually detectable changes that improve our ability to decipher the mechanism of a perturbagen. This integration creates powerful validation loops. When we see mitochondrial fragmentation in Cell Painting, we can ask whether the metabolomics show impaired respiration and whether the transcriptomics show stress response pathway activation. Concordance across modalities dramatically increases confidence; discordance points to interesting biology worth investigating. For our DILI research, we're pursuing exactly this kind of integration — correlating morphological signatures in liver organoids with transcriptomics and clinical phenotypes. The goal is triangulation: no single data type is definitive, but convergent evidence across modalities builds a case for a mechanism that any single approach would miss. One practical advantage of Cell Painting is that it is non-destructive: the same cells can later be harvested for molecular profiling, allowing true paired measurements from identical samples. From your perspective, what are the key steps needed to standardize Cell Painting across the pharmaceutical industry so that it becomes a routine part of early drug discovery pipelines? Industry-wide adoption requires infrastructure, not just enthusiasm. Reference datasets: The JUMP-CP consortium has made enormous progress here, providing annotated compound libraries with standardized profiles. These serve as ground truth for benchmarking and enable labs to calibrate their own data against community standards. Protocol harmonization: We need validated standard operating procedures that specify dye concentrations, cell seeding density, passage range, staining timing, and imaging parameters. The sensitivity of Cell Painting to these variables means that approximately the same protocol can yield incomparable data. Analysis pipeline standardization: Agreement on feature extraction (CellProfiler remains the standard), normalization approaches using Cytominer, and output formats enable data sharing. The JUMP-CP profiling recipes we use provide a template, but adoption needs to be broader. Quality control metrics: The field needs consensus quality control metrics specific to morphological profiling — not just image quality but profile reproducibility, positive control separation, and batch effect magnitude. Poor data should be automatically flagged before contaminating downstream analysis. Single-cell quality control is often overlooked and segmentation errors, debris, and cells touching the edges of images should all be culled from datasets before downstream analysis. The methods for detecting quality issues are maturing rapidly and are converging on standardized approaches. Validation against clinical outcomes: Ultimately, the value proposition for pharma is predictive accuracy of clinical outcomes. We need prospective studies demonstrating that Cell Painting signatures predict clinical toxicity or efficacy better than alternatives. Looking ahead, how do you envision the evolution of Cell Painting assays in the next decade, particularly with advancements in automation and data analytics? The convergence of Cell Painting with AI will define the next era. Deep learning representation: We are moving away from hand-engineered features that measure predefined shape, intensity, and texture, toward learned representations where neural networks extract optimal features directly from raw pixels, such as DeepProfiler and DinoV3. Early results suggest these models capture subtle biological nuances that traditional feature sets often miss. Predictive toxicology: Models trained on massive Cell Painting databases, linked to clinical outcome data, will increasingly predict human toxicity before animal or human testing. This aligns with regulatory movement toward new approach methodologies (NAMs) and will transform how safety is assessed early in development. This will improve drug safety overall for clinical trial participants and for patients after drugs get FDA approved. Additionally, if NAMs can reduce failure rates in drug development, they could substantially lower the cost of bringing new drugs to market, helping to make medicines more affordable. Automated target deconvolution: Matching an unknown compound’s phenotype to a database of known mechanisms will become a standard, powerful approach — using learned embeddings to infer its mechanism of action instead of relying on years of traditional biochemical characterization. Closed-loop experimentation: I anticipate fully automated systems where AI analyzes screening results and independently designs follow-up experiments — selecting compounds for confirmation, adjusting dose ranges, and scheduling orthogonal assays — with minimal human intervention. Integration with spatial technologies: Combining Cell Painting with spatial transcriptomics and imaging mass cytometry, technologies my lab is actively developing, will provide unprecedented resolution on how drugs alter tissue architecture and cell-cell interactions in complex in vitro model systems like patient-derived organoids. Where do you want to see your research go in the next few years? My goal is to close the gap between throughput and physiological prediction. High-content screening has historically traded relevance for scale where immortalized or cancer cell lines in 2D enable large-scale screens but poorly predict human outcomes. Over the next few years, my team is working to establish Cell Painting in patient-derived organoid systems as a validated, regulatory-ready platform. For DILI specifically, this means demonstrating that morphological signatures in liver organoids predict clinical hepatotoxicity patterns with accuracy that influences drug development decisions. The technical components — high-content imaging with our Yokogawa systems, CellPose and CellProfiler segmentation and feature extraction pipelines, and ML classifiers — have matured to the point where we can accurately predict clinical outcomes. The frontier is validation: showing prospectively that these platforms predict clinical outcomes better than existing in vitro and in vivo approaches. That's the work that will make Cell Painting not just useful for interrogating cellular systems in the laboratory, but actually transformative for producing safer, more effective therapeutics to patients. With consistent geometry and mixing design, bench-to-commercial bioreactor translation is becoming predictable. Written by Trevor J Henderson Trevor J Henderson Trevor Henderson is the Creative Services Director for the Laboratory Products Group at LabX Media Group. With over two decades of experience, he specializes in scientific and technical writing, editing, View Full Profile Learn about our Editorial Policies . Jun 4, 2026 | 7 min read The challenge of bioreactor scale-up is not biological: cells do not know how large the vessel around them is. The challenge is hydrodynamic. Maintaining consistent oxygen transfer, mixing uniformity, and shear stress profiles as vessel volume increases by three orders of magnitude is the engineering problem that scale-up criteria, geometric design, and scale-down modeling are all built to solve. Flow (2026) Download PDF Register for free to listen to this article Listen with Speechify 0:00 7:00 Highlights in this article Why scale-up fails: the physics of increasing volume The engineering criteria of bioreactor scale-up Geometric similarity: engineering predictability into the vessel design Scale-down models: predicting commercial behavior at bench scale N-1 perfusion: redefining the inoculation density Process analytical technology in scale-up verification Most bioreactor scale-up failures are not scientific failures. They are engineering failures. The biology that worked at 5 liters, including the cell line, the media, the feeding strategy, and the dissolved oxygen setpoint, is sound. What changes between the bench bioreactor and the 2,000-liter production vessel is the physics of the environment surrounding those cells, and if those changes are not anticipated and engineered for, the process that looked excellent at small scale will behave unexpectedly at large scale. The parameters that govern cell culture productivity do not scale linearly with volume. Mixing time, oxygen transfer rate, CO2 accumulation, and shear stress distribution all change in ways that can stress cells, alter product quality attributes, and create batch-to-batch variability that raises regulatory questions. Understanding how and why these parameters change and designing scale-up strategies to control them is the technical foundation of predictable scale-up. This article covers the engineering principles of bioreactor scale-up, from the dimensionless criteria used to design consistent hydrodynamic environments to the role of N-1 perfusion in redefining inoculation density. For the facility design context in which this scale-up engineering operates, see the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities , and for the broader bioprocessing lifecycle from development through commercial manufacturing, see the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . Read More Why scale-up fails: the physics of increasing volume When a bioreactor volume increases by a factor of 1,000, from 5 liters to 5,000 liters, the linear dimensions of the vessel increase by only the cube root of 1,000, approximately 10-fold. That geometric relationship governs everything about how the hydrodynamics of the culture change, and most of those changes make the engineering problem harder. Mixing time, the time required for a pulse addition to be uniformly distributed throughout the vessel, increases with scale under constant volumetric power input. In a 5-liter bioreactor, a base pulse from the pH control loop may homogenize in seconds. In a 2,000-liter vessel, the same pulse may create a transient pH gradient that exposes cells in the vicinity of the addition point to conditions outside the setpoint range for tens of seconds before bulk mixing restores uniformity. Cells exposed to repeated pH excursions can shift glycosylation patterns and charge variant profiles, potentially affecting critical quality attributes of the drug substance. Dissolved CO2 accumulation is another scale-dependent challenge. In large-scale bioreactors, the hydrostatic pressure at the bottom of a tall vessel increases the partial pressure of dissolved CO2 beyond levels typically encountered at bench scale, and bubbles have a longer residence time in the culture as they rise through a deeper liquid column. Elevated pCO2 can inhibit cell growth and alter glycosylation, and the CO2 stripping strategy that works at 5 liters may be insufficient at 2,000 liters. Shear stress distribution also changes. Impeller tip speed, which correlates with the shear forces cells experience near the agitator, scales with impeller diameter and rotation speed. Maintaining a constant tip speed at large scale while also maintaining adequate mixing requires impeller design choices that become increasingly complex as vessel volume increases. Research published in Biotechnology Progress in 2025 confirmed that hydrodynamic conditions, including volumetric power input, impeller configuration, and aeration strategy, are among the most significant determinants of production yield during CHO fed-batch scale-up, and that no single criterion adequately captures the full complexity of the scale-up problem. The engineering criteria of bioreactor scale-up Scale-up engineering uses dimensionless or volume-normalized criteria to design bioreactor operating conditions that maintain consistent hydrodynamic environments as vessel scale increases. No single criterion perfectly captures the full complexity of scale-up, and in practice, scale-up engineers must choose which criterion to prioritize based on the process requirements and the cell line's specific sensitivities. Criterion What it controls How it is maintained Key trade-off at large scale P/V (volumetric power input) Mixing energy per unit volume; shear stress distribution Constant agitation power per unit volume as vessel scale increases Maintaining P/V at large scale requires higher tip speeds, increasing shear stress risk for sensitive cell lines kLa (oxygen transfer coefficient) Rate of oxygen delivery from gas to culture; critical at high viable cell density Combined adjustment of agitation rate, sparge gas flow, and sparger design to maintain target kLa Higher gas flows increase foaming and CO2 stripping; bubble coalescence behavior changes with vessel geometry Tip speed Local shear near impeller blade; primary shear stress experienced by cells Constant impeller peripheral velocity across scales Conflicts with P/V criterion at large scale; requires impeller diameter and geometry optimization Mixing time (tm) Time for complete homogenization; determines pH and DO gradient severity Geometric similarity and optimized impeller configuration Inherently increases with volume; spatial heterogeneity in large bioreactors can affect critical quality attributes vvm (volumetric gas flow rate) Total gas delivery per unit culture volume; CO2 stripping capacity Constant gas volume per culture volume per minute CO2 accumulates with increasing vessel height; bubble behavior changes with hydrostatic pressure at depth In practice, maintaining constant P/V is the most widely used primary scale-up criterion for mammalian cell culture because it most directly controls the mixing environment and is most predictive of cell culture performance. kLa is typically verified as a secondary criterion to confirm adequate oxygen delivery at the target agitation and gassing conditions. Tip speed is monitored as a constraint: if the tip speed required to maintain P/V at large scale exceeds the shear sensitivity threshold of the cell line, the impeller design must be revised. Read More Geometric similarity: engineering predictability into the vessel design The most reliable foundation for predictable scale-up is geometric similarity across the full volume range of a bioreactor platform. When key geometric ratios, including the height-to-diameter ratio of the vessel (H/D), the ratio of impeller diameter to tank diameter (d/D), and the impeller off-bottom clearance, are held constant from 5 liters to 5,000 liters, the dimensionless hydrodynamic behavior of the culture scales predictably. The kLa, mixing time, and shear profiles calculated or measured at bench scale will translate to large scale without requiring empirical re-optimization of every operating parameter. This principle is why modern single-use bioreactor platforms designed for process development through commercial manufacturing maintain consistent geometric ratios across their volume range. A development bioreactor and a production bioreactor from the same platform family, operating at the same impeller rotation speed in revolutions per minute per liter of culture, will produce similar hydrodynamic environments because the geometry that generates those environments is consistent. Scale-up becomes a matter of calculating the correct operating parameters for the new volume, rather than re-characterizing the process from scratch. For single-use bioreactors, bag geometry is as important as vessel geometry. The working volume fraction of the bag, the aspect ratio of the inflated bag at maximum fill, and the film architecture, meaning the layered polymer construction of the bag itself, affect both the hydrodynamic environment inside the vessel and the extractables profile of the bag material in contact with the drug substance. Consistent film specifications across a platform's volume range are a prerequisite for assuming that extractables data generated at small scale will be representative of large-scale production conditions. Scale-down models: predicting commercial behavior at bench scale Designing a scale-down model that accurately predicts the behavior of a large-scale production bioreactor is one of the most valuable investments a process development team can make. A 2025 study published in the Journal of Biological Engineering documented successful scale-up of CHO cell cultures across three orders of magnitude, from 96-well microtiter plates through stirred-tank bioreactors, by carefully matching oxygen transfer rates and mixing conditions at each scale. The study confirmed that oxygen transfer rate, not simply agitation speed, is the critical parameter for maintaining cell culture performance across scale transitions. A scale-down model for a 2,000-liter production bioreactor is typically a 10- to 15-liter bioreactor operated to mimic the kLa, mixing time, and pH and DO control dynamics of the large-scale vessel. For processes sensitive to pH heterogeneity, scale-down heterogeneity models deliberately introduce controlled pH or dissolved oxygen gradients that simulate the transient excursions cells experience in a large vessel where base pulses do not distribute instantaneously. These models allow process development scientists to evaluate the impact of large-scale heterogeneity on cell performance and product quality without consuming the time and resources of a full-scale run. Read More Miniaturized bioreactor systems operating at 15 to 250 milliliters enable high-throughput screening of operating conditions, cell lines, and media formulations with consistent hydrodynamic control in a parallel format. These systems are most valuable in early process development, where large numbers of conditions must be evaluated quickly. Their role in scale-up validation is more limited: they can confirm parameter sensitivity and establish media and feeding optima, but a 15-milliliter vessel cannot faithfully reproduce the CO2 accumulation and mixing time dynamics of a 2,000-liter production bioreactor. N-1 perfusion: redefining the inoculation density Conventional fed-batch bioreactor scale-up begins with inoculation at a viable cell density of approximately 0.5 million cells per milliliter. The culture then spends the first three to five days of the production run in a growth phase, building cell density before peak productivity is reached. That growth phase consumes bioreactor time, media, and production capacity without generating product, and any variability in the health or density of the seed material propagates directly into production bioreactor performance. N-1 perfusion changes this starting point. By running the final seed train stage in perfusion mode, continuously exchanging spent media with fresh media while retaining cells in the vessel, the N-1 bioreactor can accumulate viable cell density far beyond what is achievable in a standard batch seed. Research from Bristol Myers Squibb published in Bioengineering in 2022 demonstrated that N-1 perfusion with in-line capacitance probe control achieved 4.5-fold higher inoculation VCD than conventional batch N-1 seeding, delivering 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter to the production bioreactor versus the standard 0.5 million cells per milliliter. The production consequences are significant. A production bioreactor inoculated at 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter bypasses the slow growth phase, reaching peak viable cell density faster, maintaining higher peak VCD for longer, and generating proportionally more product in the same calendar time. A 2024 study published in Biotechnology Progress demonstrated that N-1 perfusion-enabled high inoculation density processes achieved an average 85% titer increase and 132% space-time yield increase compared to conventional low-inoculation-density fed-batch processes across six CHO cell lines expressing three different monoclonal antibodies. Integrating N-1 perfusion into scale-up design also improves the uniformity of seed material delivered to the production bioreactor, reducing run-to-run variability that can otherwise be attributed to variation in the physiological state of the inoculum rather than to true process variability at production scale. Process analytical technology in scale-up verification Process analytical technology (PAT) bridges the bench and commercial scale by providing real-time, in-process measurements of the critical parameters that scale-up engineering is designed to control. The FDA's PAT framework guidance , first published in 2004, explicitly supports the use of real-time quality monitoring rather than end-product testing and encouraged manufacturers to build process understanding through in-line and on-line measurement systems. That regulatory support has enabled the adoption of a generation of PAT tools that are now routinely deployed in both scale-down models and production bioreactors. Continue reading below... Application Note Scaling neuronal activity profiling with semi-automated electrophysiology Advanced microelectrode array and liquid handling technologies make neuronal culture screening more consistent and easier to scale. Read More In scale-up verification, PAT serves two complementary functions. At small scale, it establishes multivariate models that correlate measured process signals with cell culture performance and product quality outcomes. At large scale, it confirms that the critical process parameters defined during small-scale development are being maintained within their designed ranges, and that the performance the models predict at small scale is actually being achieved at production scale. Key PAT tools in bioreactor scale-up verification include in-line Raman spectroscopy for real-time glucose, lactate, and product concentration measurement; near-infrared spectroscopy for cell density and metabolite monitoring; and capacitance probes for viable cell density estimation without sampling. The integration of multiple PAT data streams into a unified process monitoring platform enables real-time decisions about feeding, pH adjustment, and harvest timing that would otherwise depend on discrete offline measurements taken hours apart. For context on how PAT and digital manufacturing tools integrate into the broader Pharma 4.0 framework, see the related coverage in the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 . This article was produced under Drug Discovery News' AI Editorial Guidelines Download PDF Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) What is bioreactor scale-up? Bioreactor scale-up is the process of translating a cell culture manufacturing process from a small development-scale bioreactor to progressively larger vessels, ultimately reaching commercial production scale. The goal is to maintain the same hydrodynamic environment, including oxygen transfer rate, mixing uniformity, and shear stress distribution, at each larger scale so that cell culture performance and product quality attributes are preserved. Scale-up spans from bench-scale bioreactors of 5 to 15 liters in early development through clinical-scale vessels of 50 to 500 liters and production-scale vessels of 500 to 5,000 liters. What scale-up criteria are used to design consistent bioreactor environments? The most commonly used scale-up criteria in mammalian cell culture are volumetric power input (P/V), which maintains consistent mixing energy per unit volume; the oxygen transfer coefficient (kLa), which maintains consistent oxygen delivery; and tip speed, which maintains consistent shear stress near the impeller. Mixing time is monitored as a key outcome of the design, and volumetric gas flow rate (vvm) is maintained to ensure adequate CO2 stripping. No single criterion perfectly captures all aspects of scale-up, and process engineers must balance these criteria based on the specific sensitivities of their cell line and process. Why does pH become heterogeneous in large-scale bioreactors? In large-scale bioreactors, the base solution added by the pH control loop takes time to distribute throughout the vessel after each pulse addition. During that mixing time, the region near the addition point experiences a transient pH elevation before bulk mixing restores uniformity. In a 5-liter bioreactor, mixing may be complete in seconds. In a 2,000-liter vessel, mixing time under equivalent volumetric power input is longer, creating more significant and more prolonged pH gradients. Cells repeatedly exposed to these transient excursions can experience physiological stress that shifts glycosylation patterns and charge variant profiles, affecting critical quality attributes of the drug substance. What is N-1 perfusion and how does it improve bioreactor scale-up? N-1 perfusion runs the final stage of the seed train in perfusion mode, continuously exchanging spent media for fresh media while retaining cells in the vessel, allowing the seed culture to accumulate viable cell densities of 20 to 80 million cells per milliliter before inoculating the production bioreactor. Conventional batch N-1 seeding delivers inoculation densities of approximately 0.5 million cells per milliliter to the production bioreactor. N-1 perfusion has been shown to enable inoculation at 2 to 10 million cells per milliliter, a four- to 20-fold improvement that shortens the production bioreactor growth phase, increases peak viable cell density, and improves volumetric productivity. Published studies report titer increases of 85% or more from N-1 perfusion-enabled high inoculation density processes. What makes a good scale-down model for a production bioreactor? A good scale-down model matches the key hydrodynamic parameters of the large-scale production bioreactor, including kLa, mixing time, and the CO2 stripping characteristics of the gassing system, at a volume small enough to run in parallel with other development experiments. Beyond basic hydrodynamic matching, effective scale-down models for large-scale processes often incorporate deliberate pH or dissolved oxygen gradients that simulate the heterogeneity cells experience in large vessels, allowing development scientists to evaluate the impact of large-scale mixing limitations on cell performance and product quality without conducting a full-scale run. How does geometric similarity support bioreactor scale-up? Geometric similarity means maintaining consistent ratios of key vessel dimensions, including the vessel height-to-diameter ratio, the ratio of impeller diameter to vessel diameter, and impeller clearance from the vessel bottom, across all scales of a bioreactor platform. When these ratios are held constant, the dimensionless hydrodynamic behavior of the culture scales predictably with volume. The kLa, mixing time, and shear profiles at bench scale translate reliably to large scale, and operating conditions for new volumes can be calculated rather than empirically re-characterized from scratch. This is why bioreactor platforms designed with consistent geometry across their volume range provide more predictable scale-up than platforms where geometry varies by scale. Feb 10, 2026 | 8 min read Exploring how AI interprets cellular images to speed up drug discovery. credit: istock.com/Spectral-Design Download PDF Jonathan Sexton studies drug-induced liver injury and liver organoids, using high-content imaging, cell painting, and AI/ML to advance drug discovery. Credit: Jonathan Sexton Drug discovery is entering an era defined by unprecedented resolution in understanding cellular behavior. Traditional approaches often focus on one or a few biomarkers, giving a narrow view of how a compound affects cells. But recent advances in high-content imaging and computational biology are enabling a more holistic perspective — capturing the complexity of cellular responses in a single experiment. One technique at the forefront of this shift is Cell Painting, a morphological profiling assay that visualizes multiple cellular structures simultaneously using fluorescent dyes. By generating rich, high-dimensional data on organelle organization, shape, and texture, Cell Painting moves beyond hypothesis-driven screening, offering an unbiased window into cellular phenotypes. This allows researchers not only to identify potential drug effects and toxicity earlier but also to uncover unexpected mechanisms of action and opportunities for drug repurposing. To explore how Cell Painting is reshaping the landscape of drug discovery, DDN spoke with Jonathan Sexton , Associate Professor of Internal Medicine and Medicinal Chemistry at the University of Michigan, about the science behind the method, its practical applications in the lab, and the challenges and opportunities it presents for translating cellular insights into safer, more effective therapeutics. What is Cell Painting and why is it important for drug discovery? Cell Painting is a morphological profiling assay that uses a multiplexed set of fluorescent dyes to visualize specific cellular compartments — nucleus, nucleoli, endoplasmic reticulum (ER), mitochondria, Golgi apparatus, cytoskeleton, and plasma membrane — simultaneously. What makes it fundamentally different from traditional high-content screening is its unbiased, hypothesis-free nature. Rather than designing an assay around a specific target or biomarker, we let the biology speak for itself. In drug discovery, this shift in philosophy is transformative. Instead of asking "does this drug inhibit kinase X?" we ask "what is the comprehensive cellular response to this compound?" This approach is particularly powerful for drug repurposing, one of my core research focuses, because compounds with unexpected activities in one disease context often reveal therapeutic potential in another. The morphological fingerprint can identify novel mechanisms of action, flag early toxicity signals, and cluster structurally dissimilar compounds that share biological effects, all from a single assay. How does Cell Painting differentiate from traditional phenotypic assays in terms of data richness and predictive power? Traditional phenotypic assays typically measure a handful of endpoints — viability, a reporter signal, perhaps a biomarker intensity or protein translocation event. They answer narrow questions but can miss the broader cellular context. Cell Painting extracts thousands of morphological features per cell: size, shape, texture, intensity distributions, spatial relationships between organelles, etc. A single well can yield millions of measurements. This dimensionality fundamentally changes what's predictable. In my work on drug-induced liver injury using patient-derived liver organoids, for example, we can detect organelle-level perturbations — mitochondrial fragmentation, ER stress patterns, phospholipidosis signatures — long before they manifest as overt toxicity. Compounds that look identical in a viability assay may have completely distinct Cell Painting profiles, revealing different mechanisms and different risk profiles. The technique effectively converts microscopy images into high-dimensional, computable biological data that machine learning (ML) models can leverage for predictions we could not make by visual inspection alone. How is Cell Painting used in your lab? In my lab, Cell Painting serves as a primary screening modality, but we've adapted it in ways that extend well beyond standard implementations. Mechanism of action discovery: We compare novel compound fingerprints against annotated reference libraries — including the JUMP-CP consortium data — to generate mechanistic hypotheses. This is particularly valuable for repurposing candidates where the original indication tells us little about potential new uses. Patient-derived organoid platforms: We've moved beyond immortalized cell lines to apply Cell Painting to intestinal and hepatic organoids derived from patient tissue. This is technically demanding — 3D structures require different staining penetration strategies and more sophisticated segmentation — but it bridges the gap between throughput and physiological relevance. AI/ML pipeline development: We use the rich Cell Painting datasets to train ML models that can detect subtle phenotypic changes invisible to the human eye. In our work on drug-induced liver injury (DILI), we are developing classifiers that predict clinical hepatotoxicity by analyzing morphological signatures in patient-derived liver cells. These models accurately identify drugs with known DILI risk. For example, using our approach, we were able to detect significant liver toxicity in several drugs that recently failed clinical trials, including inarigivir for chronic hepatitis B. The models revealed that its toxicity was driven by mitochondrial damage, highlighting how ML predictions can uncover specific mechanisms of harm. Barrier function prediction: One of our current projects uses machine vision to predict functional outcomes in intestinal organoids for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We have developed models that can accurately detect leaky gut, a condition where the intestinal barrier is compromised, allowing bacterial antigens to cross into the body and trigger inflammation — a key driver of IBD. By linking Cell Painting morphological features with measurements of barrier integrity (transepithelial electrical resistance), we created a predictive model that can guide drug discovery for IBD by identifying compounds that improve intestinal barrier function. What are some of the challenges or limitations of working with Cell Painting today? Several practical challenges persist despite the technique's maturation: Data infrastructure: A single large screen generates terabytes of images and hundreds of gigabytes of tabular data. We run our analysis using CellProfiler pipelines that output parquet files for downstream processing, but storage, versioning, and compute resources remain significant operational challenges. Batch effects: Cell Painting is very sensitive to experimental variation — staining duration, reagent lots, cell passage, even plate position effects. These batch effects can obscure true biological signals. We've invested heavily in normalization strategies and plate design to mitigate this, but it requires constant vigilance. Biological interpretation: We can extract a feature called "radial distribution of ER intensity at 50 percent radius" and detect how they change in response to a compound, but interpreting what these changes mean biologically remains challenging. The field is improving at linking specific feature patterns to known cellular processes, but much work remains. Combining Cell Painting with high-throughput transcriptomics can help reveal the underlying mechanisms, but it takes significant expertise to translate these data into a clear, interpretable molecular mechanism of action. Translating to complex models: Applying standardized Cell Painting protocols to organoids introduces new variables: penetration depth, optical sectioning requirements, segmentation of irregular 3D structures. The protocols that work beautifully in 2D monolayers require substantial optimization for our 3D patient-derived organoid systems. Cell Painting as a technique is around a decade old now. How has this tool improved over that time? The evolution has been remarkable, driven by improvements in high-content imaging hardware, biology and chemistry tools, and advancements in computational approaches for analysis. Imaging throughput: We use modern high-content imaging systems, specifically the Yokogawa Cell Voyager 8000 (CV8000), which allow rapid collection of high-quality images. The CV8000 uses water immersion objective lenses that greatly improve spatial resolution and signal-to-background ratios, and its four scientific CMOS (complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor) cameras capture four channels at the same time. Older Nipkow confocal spinning disc systems, by contrast, suffered from a drastic loss of signal that made them unusable for dyes/stains that weren’t very bright. The Yokogawa dual microlens spinning disc focuses light more efficiently through the pinholes, producing stronger signals even from weaker dyes. This lets us image faster, achieve higher resolution, and maintain robust signal intensity without compromise. 3D model compatibility: The adaptation to organoids and spheroids represents perhaps the most important biological advance. Early Cell Painting was validated exclusively in 2D immortalized lines. We're now successfully applying it to patient-derived 3D cultures, which introduces challenges in staining penetration and confocal imaging requirements but gains physiological relevance that dramatically improves translational value. Reagent improvements: Dye formulations are now more stable, and innovations like the Mitsui gas-permeable InnoCell plates — which we are testing for organoid experiments — help maintain high-quality 3D structures across large-scale screens. Analysis infrastructure: Nuclear and cellular segmentation has improved dramatically thanks to neural networks such as the CellPose 4 SAM model, which can achieve nearly perfect segmentation automatically, without any user input. Additionally, the JUMP-CP consortium has established reference datasets and standardized analysis workflows that didn’t exist five years ago, greatly improving our ability to compare data across instruments and batches. At the same time, CellProfiler has matured, and the field has developed widely accepted approaches for normalization and quality control. How do you see Cell Painting integrating with omics technologies such as transcriptomics, proteomics, or metabolomics to create a more holistic view of cellular states? Cell Painting provides something the omics technologies cannot: direct visualization of the phenotypic outcome of a perturbation, whether that be a small molecule drug or a genetic perturbation like CRISPR interference. Transcriptomics captures what the cell plans to do, proteomics informs what machinery the cell has available, and metabolomics indicates what reactions are occurring. Cell Painting shows the phenotypic result of a perturbation that anchors the analysis of other omics technologies with visually detectable changes that improve our ability to decipher the mechanism of a perturbagen. This integration creates powerful validation loops. When we see mitochondrial fragmentation in Cell Painting, we can ask whether the metabolomics show impaired respiration and whether the transcriptomics show stress response pathway activation. Concordance across modalities dramatically increases confidence; discordance points to interesting biology worth investigating. For our DILI research, we're pursuing exactly this kind of integration — correlating morphological signatures in liver organoids with transcriptomics and clinical phenotypes. The goal is triangulation: no single data type is definitive, but convergent evidence across modalities builds a case for a mechanism that any single approach would miss. One practical advantage of Cell Painting is that it is non-destructive: the same cells can later be harvested for molecular profiling, allowing true paired measurements from identical samples. From your perspective, what are the key steps needed to standardize Cell Painting across the pharmaceutical industry so that it becomes a routine part of early drug discovery pipelines? Industry-wide adoption requires infrastructure, not just enthusiasm. Reference datasets: The JUMP-CP consortium has made enormous progress here, providing annotated compound libraries with standardized profiles. These serve as ground truth for benchmarking and enable labs to calibrate their own data against community standards. Protocol harmonization: We need validated standard operating procedures that specify dye concentrations, cell seeding density, passage range, staining timing, and imaging parameters. The sensitivity of Cell Painting to these variables means that approximately the same protocol can yield incomparable data. Analysis pipeline standardization: Agreement on feature extraction (CellProfiler remains the standard), normalization approaches using Cytominer, and output formats enable data sharing. The JUMP-CP profiling recipes we use provide a template, but adoption needs to be broader. Quality control metrics: The field needs consensus quality control metrics specific to morphological profiling — not just image quality but profile reproducibility, positive control separation, and batch effect magnitude. Poor data should be automatically flagged before contaminating downstream analysis. Single-cell quality control is often overlooked and segmentation errors, debris, and cells touching the edges of images should all be culled from datasets before downstream analysis. The methods for detecting quality issues are maturing rapidly and are converging on standardized approaches. Validation against clinical outcomes: Ultimately, the value proposition for pharma is predictive accuracy of clinical outcomes. We need prospective studies demonstrating that Cell Painting signatures predict clinical toxicity or efficacy better than alternatives. Looking ahead, how do you envision the evolution of Cell Painting assays in the next decade, particularly with advancements in automation and data analytics? The convergence of Cell Painting with AI will define the next era. Deep learning representation: We are moving away from hand-engineered features that measure predefined shape, intensity, and texture, toward learned representations where neural networks extract optimal features directly from raw pixels, such as DeepProfiler and DinoV3. Early results suggest these models capture subtle biological nuances that traditional feature sets often miss. Predictive toxicology: Models trained on massive Cell Painting databases, linked to clinical outcome data, will increasingly predict human toxicity before animal or human testing. This aligns with regulatory movement toward new approach methodologies (NAMs) and will transform how safety is assessed early in development. This will improve drug safety overall for clinical trial participants and for patients after drugs get FDA approved. Additionally, if NAMs can reduce failure rates in drug development, they could substantially lower the cost of bringing new drugs to market, helping to make medicines more affordable. Automated target deconvolution: Matching an unknown compound’s phenotype to a database of known mechanisms will become a standard, powerful approach — using learned embeddings to infer its mechanism of action instead of relying on years of traditional biochemical characterization. Closed-loop experimentation: I anticipate fully automated systems where AI analyzes screening results and independently designs follow-up experiments — selecting compounds for confirmation, adjusting dose ranges, and scheduling orthogonal assays — with minimal human intervention. Integration with spatial technologies: Combining Cell Painting with spatial transcriptomics and imaging mass cytometry, technologies my lab is actively developing, will provide unprecedented resolution on how drugs alter tissue architecture and cell-cell interactions in complex in vitro model systems like patient-derived organoids. Where do you want to see your research go in the next few years? My goal is to close the gap between throughput and physiological prediction. High-content screening has historically traded relevance for scale where immortalized or cancer cell lines in 2D enable large-scale screens but poorly predict human outcomes. Over the next few years, my team is working to establish Cell Painting in patient-derived organoid systems as a validated, regulatory-ready platform. For DILI specifically, this means demonstrating that morphological signatures in liver organoids predict clinical hepatotoxicity patterns with accuracy that influences drug development decisions. The technical components — high-content imaging with our Yokogawa systems, CellPose and CellProfiler segmentation and feature extraction pipelines, and ML classifiers — have matured to the point where we can accurately predict clinical outcomes. The frontier is validation: showing prospectively that these platforms predict clinical outcomes better than existing in vitro and in vivo approaches. That's the work that will make Cell Painting not just useful for interrogating cellular systems in the laboratory, but actually transformative for producing safer, more effective therapeutics to patients. Jun 4, 2026 | 7 min read The challenge of bioreactor scale-up is not biological: cells do not know how large the vessel around them is. The challenge is hydrodynamic. Maintaining consistent oxygen transfer, mixing uniformity, and shear stress profiles as vessel volume increases by three orders of magnitude is the engineering problem that scale-up criteria, geometric design, and scale-down modeling are all built to solve. They are engineering failures. The biology that worked at 5 liters, including the cell line, the media, the feeding strategy, and the dissolved oxygen setpoint, is sound. What changes between the bench bioreactor and the 2,000-liter production vessel is the physics of the environment surrounding those cells, and if those changes are not anticipated and engineered for, the process that looked excellent at small scale will behave unexpectedly at large scale. The parameters that govern cell culture productivity do not scale linearly with volume. Mixing time, oxygen transfer rate, CO2 accumulation, and shear stress distribution all change in ways that can stress cells, alter product quality attributes, and create batch-to-batch variability that raises regulatory questions. Understanding how and why these parameters change and designing scale-up strategies to control them is the technical foundation of predictable scale-up. This article covers the engineering principles of bioreactor scale-up, from the dimensionless criteria used to design consistent hydrodynamic environments to the role of N-1 perfusion in redefining inoculation density. For the facility design context in which this scale-up engineering operates, see the blueprint for single-use biomanufacturing facilities , and for the broader bioprocessing lifecycle from development through commercial manufacturing, see the ultimate guide to bioprocessing scale-up and Pharma 4.0 .
